newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Gulf ups Clyde stake to 27 pct in raid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gulf ups Clyde stake to 27 pct in raid.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources took a major step forward in its hostile battle for Clyde Petroleum on Tuesday by raising its stake to 27.88 percent and analysts said hopes of a counter bid were fading.
Gulf Canada said it bought 114.9 million shares from a range of institutional and other investors, increasing its stake in Clyde from only 7.14 percent on Monday.
Gulf's offer of 120 pence ($1.96) per share closes at 1300 GMT on February 18. The company raised its bid from an initial offer of 105 pence which was widely considered to be too low.
Dealers said stock broker Cazenove had been buying Clyde shares on behalf of Gulf Canada. "Cazenove have been hoovering up shares," one said.
Fund manager CIN management said it had sold around 13 million Clyde shares on Tuesday.
Clyde was the most heavily-traded share on the London stock market and closed unchanged at Gulf's offer price of 120 pence.

"The decision by shareholders to sell reinforces Gulf Canada's belief that its offer is full and fair and demonstrates that the market now accepts there will be no counter bidder," Gulf said in a statement.
Analysts said they believed there is now a good chance Gulf Canada will succeed in its bid.
"They only need support of one or two of the major shareholders and then they've got it basically," said one leading analyst.
Four institutional shareholders -- Schroders Plc, PDFM Limited, Capital Group Companies Inc and Norwich Union -- hold more than 50 percent of Clyde.
But with a 28 percent stake under its belt, Gulf no longer needs to convince all of these major shareholders in order to gain control over Clyde.
Analyst said many Clyde investors may be driven into Gulf Canada's arms after recent steep falls in crude oil prices.
Shares in oil explorations firms such as Clyde are tightly linked to moves in crude prices.
"Gulf is playing on fears now that there won't be a white knight, that one or two of the big shareholders will accept and that the whole sector will go down as oil prices slip," another analyst said.
"If a white knight comes in now they have blown it. They should have stepped in immediately after Gulf raised its offer to stop investors selling to Gulf," he added.
Clyde has repeatedly said Gulf Canada's offer undervalued the company as it engaged in an increasingly bitter war of words with Gulf over its worth.
Hopes of a white knight had centred on North America, where the habit of valuing oil exploration and production firms on the basis of their cashflow multiples makes Clyde look very attractive.
The oil sector is also relatively cash-rich after years of cost-cutting.
